summary: Danish Penal Code violations are punishable by up to 60 day-fines, with the fine halved (minimum DKK 500, about USD 73 in 2024) for offenders under 18 or whose gross annual income does not exceed DKK 171,795 (2020), giving a lower severity ceiling than Germany/Finland plus an explicit income-based reduction band.
label_raw: up to 60 day-units; halve if gross income <= DKK 171,795/yr or under 18; floor DKK 500
source_citation: Wikipedia 'Day-fine' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day-fine), verbatim: 'may be punishable by up to 60 day-fines'; reduced 'by half (to a minimum of DKK 500)' for offenders under 18 or 'whose gross annual income does not exceed DKK 171,795 (as of 2020)'. DKK 500 ~ USD 73 (DKK->USD x0.145, 2024).

summary: A Finnish businessman was fined EUR 112,000 (about USD 160,000 in 2024 after FX and inflation) in 2009 for driving 82 km/h in a 60 km/h zone, illustrating how the same trivial-harm offence scales to six figures purely via the income-indexed per-unit value.
label_raw: speeding 82 in 60 km/h zone; EUR 112,000 fine
source_citation: Wikipedia 'Day-fine' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day-fine), verbatim: 'In 2009 a businessman was fined EUR 112,000 for travelling at 82 kilometres per hour in an area with a speed limit of 60 kilometres per hour.' (~USD 160,000 normalized to 2024 via EUR x1.08 + ~30% cumulative inflation 2009-2024; the USD figure is the collector's estimate, not a sourced number).

summary: A Finnish day-fine equals about half of daily disposable income, where disposable income is ~1/60 of monthly net income after a EUR 255 living allowance, with a EUR 6 floor per unit; a single offence carries 1 to 120 day-units (240 if multiple offences combined) and a speeding fine is at least EUR 115, separating income-scaled money from severity-scaled count.
label_raw: day-unit = 1/2 of (monthly net /60) after EUR 255 allowance; range 1-120 units (240 combined); floor EUR 6/unit; speeding min EUR 115
source_citation: Wikipedia 'Day-fine' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day-fine), verbatim: 'the day-fine is one half of daily disposable income ... one 60th part of the person's monthly mean income ... after ... a basic living allowance of EUR 255'; 'minimum of 1 day-fine, up to a maximum of 120 day-fines ... 240 day-fines' if combined; 'minimum amount of a day-fine is 6 euros'; 'For speeding ... the fine is at least ... EUR 115' (~USD 124 in 2024).

summary: A Finnish (Nokia) businessman with a ~EUR 10 million yearly income received only 6 day-units in 2001 but a total of EUR 26,000 (about USD 43,000 in 2024) for running a red light, showing that with severity (unit count) held very low the total money is set almost entirely by income.
source_citation: Wikipedia 'Day-fine' (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day-fine), verbatim: 'a Finnish businessman with a yearly income of 10 million euros, received a relatively mild punishment of six day-fines, amounting EUR 26,000' for running a red light. (~USD 43,000 normalized to 2024; USD figure is the collector's estimate.)

summary: Finnish multimillionaire Anders Wiklof was fined EUR 121,000 (about USD 131,000 in 2024) in 2023 for driving 82 km/h in a 50 km/h zone, a single low-severity offence whose few day-units became enormous solely because the per-unit value tracks his very high income (no cap).
label_raw: speeding 82 in 50 km/h zone; EUR 121,000 fine + 10-day licence suspension
source_citation: ABC News (abcnews.com/ABCNews/finnish-businessman-handed-121000-speeding-ticket, story id 99861907, 2023): fine 'EUR 121,000', '82 kilometers per hour ... 50 km/h' zone (Aland), plus a 10-day driving-licence suspension; report also notes a prior EUR 63,680 fine (2013) and an earlier EUR 95,000 fine. CAUTION: the original collector citation transposed the prior-fine years/amounts ('EUR 63,000 (2018) and EUR 95,000 (2013)') -- per ABC the 2013 fine was EUR 63,680 and the EUR 95,000 fine was several years earlier (~2008); the headline 2023 figure is correct.

summary: German day-unit counts form an empirical severity ladder: ~42% of 2018 fine cases were under 30 units and ~49% were 31-90 units, and a fine over 90 daily units is the threshold above which the conviction appears on the certificate of conduct (Fuehrungszeugnis), pricing relative offence seriousness on the 5-360 scale.
label_raw: ordinary offences 30-90 units; >90 units = entry on Fuehrungszeugnis (criminal record)
source_citation: Mitali Nagrecha, 'The Limits of Fairer Fines: Lessons from Germany' (Criminal Justice Policy Program, Harvard Law School / Fines and Fees Justice Center, 2020), finesandfeesjusticecenter.org: '42% of all cases ... less than 30 units and another 49% ... between 31 and 90 units'. Record threshold: German Federal Office of Justice (bundesjustizamt.de) / criminal-law-germany.lawyer 'When do I have a criminal record in Germany?': fines of '90 daily rates or more' are entered on the Fuehrungszeugnis.

summary: German StGB Section 40 sets a fine as 5 to 360 daily units (severity/culpability), each unit valued from EUR 1 to EUR 30,000 (about USD 1 to USD 32,400 in 2024) based on the offender's net income per day; the count encodes severity and the per-unit value encodes the money metric.
label_raw: StGB Section 40 daily-unit count (5-360) and unit value (EUR 1-30,000)
source_citation: German Criminal Code (StGB) Section 40, lewik.org/term/15370 (verbatim: 'minimum fine shall consist of five and ... maximum ... three hundred and sixty full daily units'; 'A daily unit shall not be set at less than one and not at more than thirty thousand euros') and official translation gesetze-im-internet.de/englisch_stgb.

summary: In Germany an unpaid day-fine converts to substitute prison time: historically 1 day-unit = 1 day in prison, and since the 1 Feb 2024 reform 2 day-units = 1 day in prison, giving an explicit legal exchange rate between roughly two days of disposable income and one day of lost liberty.
label_raw: Ersatzfreiheitsstrafe conversion: pre-2024 1 unit=1 prison day; post-2024 2 units=1 prison day
source_citation: KFN (Kriminologisches Forschungsinstitut Niedersachsen) study on the Section 43 StGB reform, en.kfn.de/research-projects/ersatzfreiheitsstrafe: conversion shifted to '2:1 ... two daily fine rates correspond to one day of imprisonment', effective 1 February 2024; previously 1:1. Corroborated by KriPoZ commentary (kripoz.de, Feb 2024).

summary: Swedish day-fines run 30 to 150 units (up to 200 for multiple offences) with each unit valued from SEK 50 to SEK 1,000 (about USD 5 to USD 95 in 2024), one unit being roughly one-thousandth of annual income; unlike Finland the per-unit value is capped, bounding the money axis.
label_raw: 30-150 units (200 combined); SEK 50-1,000 per unit; ~1/1000 of annual income; total floor SEK 750
source_citation: Swedish Penal Code (Brottsbalken) Chapter 25 on fines, as summarized by TheLocal.se (thelocal.se/20240423, 2024) and Swedish legal sources (domarbloggen.se, aklagare.se): number of day-fines 'at least thirty and at most one hundred fifty ... up to two hundred' for joint sentences; each day-fine 'a minimum of 50 kronor and a maximum of 1,000 kronor'; 'one daily fine ... equivalent to one thousandth of the yearly income'. SEK 50/1000 ~ USD 5 / USD 95 (SEK->USD x0.095, 2024). CORRECTED: collector stated SEK 30 floor; current statutory minimum is SEK 50 (the SEK 30 floor is an outdated figure). Collector's Wikipedia 'Day-fine' citation does not contain these Swedish figures and was replaced.

summary: A Swedish motorist in Switzerland in 2010 was fined CHF 3,600 per day for 300 days, more than EUR 1,000,000 total (CHF ~1.08 million; about USD 1.36 million in 2024) for driving ~290 km/h, the extreme high end showing day-unit count (300, near the ceiling) multiplied by an income-indexed per-day value can rival serious-injury compensation in magnitude.
label_raw: speeding ~290 km/h; CHF 3,600/day x 300 day-units = CHF ~1.08M (>EUR 1,000,000)
source_citation: SWI swissinfo.ch ('Driver faces $1,000,000 speeding fine', swissinfo.ch, 2010) and Euronews (2023-01-04, 'Finland's progressive punishment'): a 2010 motorist 'received 3,600 Swiss francs per day for 300 days -- that's more than a million euros in total' (CHF ~1.08M). ~USD 1.36M normalized to 2024 (CHF->USD x1.13 + inflation; USD figure is the collector's estimate).
